title: What the Book of Job Actually Says About Suffering
body:
Job is the Bible's most uncomfortable book — not because it raises the problem of evil, but because of how it answers it. Or rather, how it refuses to. Job's friends spend thirty-odd chapters explaining why he suffers, and God rebukes them for it. The message isn't that suffering has a purpose you can discern. It's that the friends' confidence in their own explanations was itself the problem.

This is harder to sit with than most Christian teaching about suffering allows. We want the framework — the reason, the lesson, the eventual good that comes from it. Job denies us that. What it offers instead is presence: the whirlwind, the voice, the unanswerable questions that somehow satisfy more than answers would have.

For anyone in a season of suffering that makes no sense, Job is not a book of comfort in the conventional sense. It is a book of honest company.

title: Ecclesiastes and the Permission to Find Life Meaningless
body:
Qohelet — 'the Teacher' — begins with one of scripture's most startling declarations: 'Vanity of vanities, all is vanity.' This is not despair dressed up in theological language. It is a careful, systematic observation that human striving — for wisdom, pleasure, wealth, legacy — does not deliver what it promises.

What makes Ecclesiastes unusual is that it doesn't then pivot to 'but God fills the gap.' It sits in the discomfort. It observes that the righteous and the wicked both die. It notes that work doesn't always reward effort. It says 'eat your food with joy and drink your wine with a merry heart, for God has already approved what you do' — which is either the Bible's best advice or its most unsettling, depending on where you are.

The book is permission, given by scripture itself, to acknowledge when life feels futile. That acknowledgement is the beginning of honest faith, not its opposite.

title: The Scandal of Jonah: Why the Prophet Wanted the Wicked to Be Destroyed
body:
Most people remember Jonah for the whale. The whale is the least interesting part. The truly difficult part comes at the end, when God spares Nineveh — the capital of Assyria, Israel's most feared enemy — and Jonah sits outside the city in furious grief. He had run from the mission not because he was afraid to preach, but because he was afraid it might work.

Jonah is a book about the limits of our compassion. About the people we have decided don't deserve mercy. About the moment when God's grace extends to someone we think has forfeited any right to it. Jonah's anger is understandable — Nineveh was genuinely brutal — and the book doesn't pretend otherwise. But it ends with a question from God that has never been answered in the text, and which each reader must answer for themselves.

title: Song of Songs and the Dignity of Desire
body:
The Song of Songs is the Bible's most ignored book in Christian tradition, which is remarkable given that it is entirely about erotic love. It was nearly excluded from the canon. Rabbinic tradition preserved it partly by reading it as allegory — the love between God and Israel. Christian interpreters followed suit, reading it as Christ and the church.

These allegorical readings are not wrong, exactly. But they can function as a way of making the book safe — of neutralising the direct, unapologetic, mutual desire it describes. The woman in the Song speaks as often and as boldly as the man. She initiates. She describes her own longing. She is not passive. This is worth noticing in a canon that is often read as having little to say about desire except 'contain it.'

The Song says something different: that desire between people who love each other is good, beautiful, and worth celebrating with the most extravagant poetry in scripture.

title: What 'Letting Jesus Live Through You' Actually Means
body:
The phrase is common in devotional language — 'let go and let God,' 'Christ in you, the hope of glory' — but what does it actually mean in practice? If the Christian life is not primarily about trying harder, being more disciplined, doing better, then what is it about?

Paul's language in Galatians is the clearest: 'I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.' This is either the most radical statement in the New Testament or a pious exaggeration. It cannot be both.

If taken seriously, it suggests that the Christian life is less about self-improvement and more about displacement — a gradual reorientation of the self's centre of gravity from 'what I want and what I can achieve' to 'what is being done in me and through me.' The difference in practice is enormous. One produces exhaustion. The other produces fruit even when the effort is not there.

title: The Bible's Narrative Arc in Plain Language
body:
Most people who read the Bible read it in fragments — a passage here, a chapter there, the Psalms when things are difficult. This is not wrong, but it misses something. The Bible is not primarily a collection of wisdom sayings or moral guidance. It is a story, and like any story, its parts make more sense in light of the whole.

The arc is roughly this: creation, fracture, rescue, restoration. Genesis describes a world made good. The fracture is immediate and its consequences compound across generation after generation. The rescue is not a quick fix — it takes millennia, unfolds through a specific people, and arrives in a form no one was expecting. And the restoration is not yet complete; the New Testament ends with a promise rather than a conclusion.

Understanding this arc changes how you read almost every individual passage. The laws of Leviticus make more sense. The violence of the conquest narratives becomes more explicable, if not less troubling. The letters of Paul are addressed to specific communities navigating a specific moment in the rescue story. And the strange, difficult book of Revelation is not a newspaper for the end times but a letter to persecuted churches about why history has a direction.

title: When Faith Feels Far Away: What the Mystics Knew
body:
The 'dark night of the soul' — the phrase comes from St John of the Cross — is not a crisis of belief. It is a specific spiritual experience in which the consolations of faith, the felt sense of God's presence, the emotional warmth that can accompany prayer, simply disappear. The practices that used to work stop working. Prayer feels like speaking into silence.

John of the Cross, and the contemplative tradition more broadly, treats this not as evidence that something has gone wrong but as evidence that something is going right. The withdrawal of consolation, he argues, is how God weans the soul from dependence on its own spiritual experiences. The goal is not the good feeling. The goal is God — and eventually those have to be separated.

This doesn't make the experience pleasant. But it provides a framework that prevents people from concluding that emptiness means absence. Sometimes it means the opposite.

title: The Sermon on the Mount as a Description, Not a Prescription
body:
The Beatitudes are usually read as instructions — 'be poor in spirit, be meek, be a peacemaker.' This reading turns the Sermon on the Mount into a very demanding to-do list, and most readers eventually give up on it or explain it away.

There is another reading, associated with Bonhoeffer and others: the Beatitudes are a description of the people of the kingdom. They are not commands to achieve a certain state but observations about what the life of grace looks like from the outside. The poor in spirit are not poor in spirit because they tried hard to be humble. They got there through encounter.

This shifts the entire sermon. It is no longer a standard to measure yourself against. It is a portrait — of the kind of person who has been genuinely changed by genuine encounter with the living God. The question it raises is not 'am I doing this?' but 'am I in the kind of relationship that produces this?'
